title: Subsidiarity (CCC 1883–1885)
hookLine: decisions should be made at the lowest level that can handle them

cards: Moses sits from morning until evening, and the line of people waiting for him never ends. Every dispute comes to him. His father-in-law, Jethro, watches for a day and says, more or less: this isn't good.
You'll wear yourself out, and these people with you. So Jethro gives him a plan, in Exodus. Choose able, honest people, set them over groups large and small, and let them settle the ordinary matters.
Only the hard cases come up to you. Moses listens, and does it. The Catechism doesn't tell this story, but it names a principle that sits beside it.

teach.b: The word is subsidiarity. The Catechism sets it inside a worry: societies need to work together, but too much intervention by the state can threaten personal freedom and initiative.
So the Church's teaching has worked out a principle. A community of a higher order shouldn't interfere in the internal life of a community of a lower order, taking over its functions.
It should support it when it needs help, and help coordinate its work with the rest of society, always toward the common good. The family does what a family can do.
The neighborhood, the parish, the town, what they can do.

teach.h: THE LARGER HELPS, IT DOESN'T SWALLOW.
teach.b: The larger body steps in to help, not to swallow. Then the Catechism holds up a model, and it isn't a theory of economics. It's how God governs.
God, it says, has not willed to reserve to himself all exercise of power. He entrusts to every creature the functions it is capable of performing, according to its own nature.
That way of governing shows great regard for human freedom, and should inspire the wisdom of those who govern communities. Last, the edges.

Subsidiarity is opposed to all forms of collectivism, and it sets limits on the state's intervention. Nor is it an excuse for the bigger body to walk away: support in time of need is part of the definition.
Yesterday's common good says what society is for. Subsidiarity says who should do it first: the closest hands that can.

how: Subsidiarity is a principle of Catholic social teaching; Catholics invoke it in debates about the roles of families, local communities, charities and governments.

games.q: you're Moses. people line up from morning to evening, and every dispute comes to you. your father-in-law says this isn't good. what do you do?
o: appoint able people to settle ordinary cases, and take the hard ones.
send everyone home to sort it out alone.
games.why: in Exodus 18, Moses takes Jethro's advice: able, honest people judge the ordinary matters, and the hard cases come to Moses.

practice: Think of a place where you tend to take over, a child's homework, a coworker's slides, a partner's way of loading the dishwasher, and ask: can they handle this?

If the answer is yes, picture yourself stepping back, hands off, available if they ask, and notice how that feels, maybe relief, maybe itchy fingers. If you pray, ask for the patience to let others do what they can.

wordCard.voice: Subsidiarity. A higher community shouldn't take over what a smaller one can do, but should help it when it needs help. The Catechism roots it in the way God shares his power. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: closest hands first. The week ran from feelings and conscience, through virtue and mercy, to the common good and subsidiarity. And that's seven days.
